title: The Anatomic Localization of Lesions in the Thalamus
subtitle: Reading thalamic stroke syndromes by arterial territory and nuclear group

points.text: The thalamus is divided into anterior, posterior, medial and lateral regions, with the intralaminar nuclei in the core.
points.quote: four regions can be distinguished in the thalamus: anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral

points.text: Thalamic names only loosely match human position: the VL nucleus is also dorsal, reaching the highest thalamic level.
points.quote: the ventrolateral (VL) nucleus is not only ventral in humans, but extends to the highest level of the thalamus

points.text: Midline, intralaminar, reticular and some ventral anterior nuclei are the nonspecific nuclei that mediate cortical alerting.
points.quote: The midline, intralaminar, reticular, and some areas of the ventral anterior nuclei mediate general cortical alerting responses

points.text: The anterior nucleus is more consistently tied to memory and executive function loss.
points.quote: Lesions of the anterior nucleus are more consistently associated with memory and executive function loss

points.text: VPL handles spinothalamic and medial lemniscus input; head receptors reach VPM through trigeminothalamic pathways.
points.quote: The ventroposterolateral nucleus processes somatosensory information conveyed by the spinothalamic tract and medial lemniscus.

points.text: Within the ventroposterior nucleus the head is anteroinferomedial and the leg posterosuperolateral, with the arm in between.
points.quote: the head is represented anteroinferomedially, whereas the leg is represented posterosuperolaterally; the arm is represented in an intermediate position

points.text: VL and ventral anterior nuclei are the keystone of two sensorimotor loops (cerebellar and basal ganglia), which lie close together in the thalamus.
points.quote: The VL and ventral anterior regions of the thalamus constitute the keystone for two large sensorimotor control loops

points.text: The oral VL receives pallidal input and projects to premotor cortex.
points.quote: The oral portion receives input from the globus pallidus and projects mostly to the premotor cortex.

points.text: The intermediate VL (VIM) receives cerebellar input and projects to primary motor cortex.
points.quote: The intermediate portion receives input from the cerebellum and projects to the precentral, primary motor cortex (area 4)

points.text: The pulvinar is the largest thalamic nucleus and an association nucleus modulating occipito-temporo-parietal cortex.
points.quote: the largest thalamic nucleus, the pulvinar, which comprises 30% of the thalamus

localizationRules.explanation: Thalamic arteries come from the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries, and their pattern varies between people.
localizationRules.quote: The thalamic arteries arise from the posterior communicating arteries and the perimesencephalic segment of the posterior cerebral arteries

localizationRules.rule: Carotid branches rarely infarct the thalamus
localizationRules.explanation: Most thalamic supply is vertebrobasilar; the anterior choroidal artery usually supplies only part of the lateral geniculate body.
localizationRules.quote: Only the lateral portion and the hilium of the lateral geniculate body are usually fed by the anterior choroidal artery

localizationRules.rule: One posterior cerebral occlusion can be bilateral
localizationRules.explanation: Paramedian vessels often arise from a single pedicle (artery of Percheron), so a unilateral PCA occlusion can give bilateral paramedian infarcts.
localizationRules.quote: Thus, unilateral posterior cerebral artery occlusions may result in bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts

localizationRules.rule: Lateral lesions can mimic internal capsule disease
localizationRules.explanation: Laterally placed lesions may disrupt the internal capsule and produce motor and sensory deficits that mask thalamic signs.
localizationRules.quote: Laterally located lesions may disrupt the internal capsule, thereby causing motor and sensory deficits

localizationRules.explanation: Except for sensory loss, unilateral thalamic lesions give transient deficits; bilateral lesions or compression can produce coma or akinetic mutism.
localizationRules.quote: Except for sensory deficits, unilateral thalamic lesions result in transient deficits.

keySyndromes.name: Paramedian territory infarct
keySyndromes.triad: Somnolent apathy or transient coma + Memory loss + Abnormalities of vertical gaze
keySyndromes.clue: Often also involves the paramedian midbrain; causes include top-of-the-basilar embolism, atheroma at the PCA origin or artery of Percheron occlusion.
keySyndromes.quote: Most often, the syndrome is composed of the clinical triad of somnolent apathy or transient coma, memory loss, and abnormalities of vertical gaze

keySyndromes.name: Thalamogeniculate (inferolateral) territory
keySyndromes.triad: Hemianesthesia + Transient slight hemiparesis + Hemiataxia + Choreoathetoid movements + Thalamic pain with dysesthesias and allodynia
keySyndromes.clue: Components of the classic Dejerine-Roussy syndrome; all findings are contralateral to the lesioned thalamus, and lacunar forms may give pure sensory or sensorimotor stroke.
keySyndromes.quote: Ischemia in this territory (ventroposterior nucleus, VL nucleus, and subthalamic region) causes some of the components of the classic thalamic syndrome

keySyndromes.name: Tuberothalamic (anterolateral) territory
keySyndromes.triad: Apathy and verbal perseveration + Anterograde memory loss + Facial paresis for emotional movement
keySyndromes.clue: Mainly neuropsychological: language impairment with left-sided lesions, hemineglect and impaired visuospatial processing with right-sided lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: Infarcts in this territory are due to thalamopolar artery lesions and result primarily in neuropsychological dysfunction

keySyndromes.name: Lateral posterior choroidal artery territory
keySyndromes.triad: Homonymous quadrantanopsia or horizontal sectoranopia + Decreased optokinetic nystagmus when the drum moves to the side of the lesion + Hemisensory loss with mild hemiparesis + Transcortical aphasia
keySyndromes.clue: A homonymous horizontal sectoranopia is particularly suggestive of lateral geniculate body involvement.
keySyndromes.quote: Homonymous quadrantanopsia, superior or inferior, or, rarely but particularly suggestive of involvement of the lateral geniculate body in this territory, a homonymous horizontal sectoranopia

keySyndromes.name: Thalamic astasia (posterolateral thalamus)
keySyndromes.triad: Transient inability to stand or sit with normal limb strength + Falling backward or toward the contralateral side + Deficit of overlearned axial and postural movements
keySyndromes.clue: Patients are alert with normal or near-normal strength; the lesions primarily involve the superoposterolateral thalamus and spare the rubral region.
keySyndromes.quote: They fall backward or toward the side contralateral to the lesion and have a deficit of overlearned motor activity

keySyndromes.name: Thalamic aphasia (dominant thalamus)
keySyndromes.triad: Reduced spontaneous speech with paraphasic errors and perseveration + Impaired auditory comprehension + Preserved repetition and reading + Distractibility
keySyndromes.clue: Would be classified as a mixed transcortical aphasia and tends to improve in a few weeks.
keySyndromes.quote: Dominant hemisphere thalamic lesions may cause a transient language disturbance (thalamic aphasia)

boardTraps.text: Paramedian lesions often extend into the midbrain and lower alertness so much that other thalamic motor or sensory findings cannot be elicited.
boardTraps.quote: Thus, other motor or sensory findings that would point to thalamic involvement cannot be elicited.

boardTraps.text: VL lesions can look like hemiplegia because the limbs are not used in automatic movements, yet purely thalamic involvement does not cause hemiparesis; capsular extension does.
boardTraps.quote: the failure to use the limbs contralateral to the lesion may convey to the examiner the false impression that the patient is hemiplegic

boardTraps.text: Small pupils reacting well to light (diencephalic pupils) occur with reticular activating system depression or involvement of both thalami.
boardTraps.quote: Depression of the reticular activating system (most often metabolic in nature) or involvement of both thalami results in small pupils

boardTraps.text: Vertical gaze palsy with thalamic lesions usually reflects extension into the upper midbrain rather than thalamic injury itself.
boardTraps.quote: vertical gaze palsies, not due to thalamic injury per se but due to extension of the lesions into the upper midbrain

boardTraps.text: Persistent memory loss in paramedian syndromes points to the dominant anterior nucleus or mammillothalamic tract; otherwise memory loss is usually partly transient.
boardTraps.quote: Persistent memory loss is observed only with damage of the dominant anterior nucleus or mammillothalamic tract

boardTraps.text: Central poststroke pain can mimic thalamic pain: delayed pain may follow parietal cortical infarcts (pseudothalamic syndrome).
boardTraps.quote: delayed pain may follow cortical parietal infarcts, particularly those in the bank of the Sylvian fissure, affecting the second somatosensory area
